Speculative decoding accelerates inference by having a small draft model propose token sequences that a large target model then verifies in parallel — the speedup depends critically on the acceptance rate, the fraction of draft tokens the target ratifies without rejection. The central question here is: when the draft and target models have been fine-tuned on different data distributions (e.g., the draft on general web text, the target on domain-specific RLHF or instruction data), how badly does the acceptance rate degrade, and can you predict or bound that degradation without running expensive empirical sweeps? The key concepts are the token-level KL divergence between draft and target distributions, the sequential compounding of rejection probabilities across a speculative window, and the distinction between marginal distribution shift versus conditional distribution shift — because what matters isn't just that the models disagree on vocabulary statistics globally, but that they disagree at the specific positions where decoding is greedy vs. uncertain. A beginner assumes that if the draft model is "close enough" in perplexity to the target on held-out data, acceptance rates will be acceptable — experts know this is wrong because perplexity averages over positions, while acceptance rate is dominated by the worst positions in a speculative chunk, particularly at syntactic branch points or domain-specific terminology where fine-tuning has moved the target distribution sharply. The deeper worry is that fine-tuning regimes like RLHF or DPO reshape the target's distribution in ways that are sparse and localized — a few tokens per response carry most of the KL mass — making the mismatch nearly invisible in aggregate metrics but catastrophic for speculative decoding's throughput guarantees.

In the matched-distribution setting, the optimal speculative window length (γ) grows with acceptance rate α roughly as γ* ≈ 1/(1−α) — so at α=0.9 you want windows around 10 tokens, and systems like DeepMind's Medusa or the original Chen et al. (2023) "Speculative Decoding" paper tune γ in the 4–8 range for well-matched draft/target pairs. Under distributional mismatch, the compounding structure changes qualitatively: if high-KL positions are sparse but lethal (driving local acceptance rates down to, say, 0.3–0.5 at domain-specific tokens), then a long window almost guarantees hitting one of those positions before verification, making the expected accepted length collapse faster than the average α would predict. The practical implication is that optimal γ should shrink under mismatch — sometimes to 2–3 tokens — because the marginal value of each additional speculative token turns negative once the window is long enough to reliably encounter a poison position. This is empirically visible in work on SpecInfer (Miao et al., 2023) and REST (He et al., 2024), where domain-shifted drafts show disproportionate throughput collapse at longer γ despite modest aggregate KL increases. What experts miss is that shortening γ alone is insufficient if the scheduler doesn't also adapt which tokens to speculate over — static window length tuned offline will mis-calibrate whenever the input distribution shifts mid-deployment, such as moving from code to prose within the same serving session. The right framework treats γ not as a fixed hyperparameter but as a per-request decision conditioned on a cheap estimate of local draft-target agreement, something close to what Leviathan et al. gesture at but don't fully operationalize for the mismatch setting.

The intuition is sound and has been partially validated: targeted fine-tuning of the draft on "alignment tax" tokens — the specific vocabulary positions where RLHF/DPO moves the target distribution — can recover substantial acceptance rate at low compute cost, since you're only correcting a thin slice of the output distribution. Online Speculative Decoding (Liu et al., 2023) demonstrates the principle by continuously updating the draft on accepted tokens from the target, effectively doing implicit targeted fine-tuning on exactly the positions where mismatch was revealed by rejection — they report recovering 10–20% acceptance rate on domain-shifted workloads with minimal update cost. The first thing that breaks is catastrophic forgetting at the fluency layer: if you fine-tune the draft aggressively on domain-specific high-KL tokens without regularization, you corrupt the draft's ability to predict mundane continuation tokens accurately, and since those tokens constitute the bulk of the speculative window, overall throughput can decrease despite acceptance rate improving at the targeted positions. The second failure mode is dataset construction — identifying the high-KL neighborhoods requires either running the target model to collect rejections (expensive) or using a proxy KL estimate from logit differences, and the proxy tends to misidentify positions because fine-tuned targets compress probability mass in ways that small draft models can't represent even after fine-tuning, a gap that LoRA-based surgical fine-tuning (rank 8–16) exacerbates by lacking the capacity to reshape attention patterns, not just output projections. Third, and most insidiously, surgical fine-tuning on a static target snapshot creates a moving-target problem in production: as the target model is updated (safety patches, capability updates), the high-KL neighborhoods shift, and a surgically fine-tuned draft can become worse than the baseline draft by confidently predicting the old target's idiosyncrasies rather than the new one's.

The right trigger signal is observed acceptance rate on a sliding window of recent requests — specifically, a CUSUM (cumulative sum control chart) detector on the acceptance rate time series, which has well-understood false-alarm and detection-delay tradeoffs and fires when the rate drops by a statistically significant margin rather than waiting for a fixed interval; this is operationally cleaner than KL estimation because it requires no access to target logits beyond what verification already produces. Online Speculative Decoding (Liu et al., 2023) uses a simpler variant — exponential moving average of acceptance rate with a threshold trigger — and finds that update latency of roughly 500–1000 accepted tokens balances adaptation speed against the cost of a draft gradient step, though this number is workload-dependent and they don't derive it from first principles. What breaks with purely reactive triggering is cold-start latency: the draft degrades for the entire detection window before an update fires, which in low-traffic deployments (few requests per minute) can mean serving degraded throughput for minutes before accumulating enough signal, suggesting a hybrid where cheap proxy KL monitoring on the target's logit statistics runs in parallel as a leading indicator.

The principled fusion framework here is Bayesian changepoint detection — specifically, the Adams & MacKay (2007) online changepoint detection algorithm, which maintains a posterior over "run length" (time since last distributional shift) and naturally weights fast noisy signals against slow reliable ones depending on the inferred shift type. Under a sudden swap, the run-length posterior collapses to near-zero immediately, causing the algorithm to heavily weight the high-variance position-level signal because recency dominates; under gradual drift, the posterior spreads over long run lengths, and the algorithm naturally down-weights the noisy per-position signal in favor of the smoothed acceptance rate — this shift-type-dependent reweighting emerges from the model rather than requiring manual tuning. Concretely, you'd represent state as a two-dimensional sufficient statistic: (rolling acceptance rate, empirical variance of per-position acceptance in the last K windows), feed both into the changepoint posterior update at each verification step, and trigger a draft update when the posterior probability of a recent changepoint exceeds a threshold like 0.85 — the K and threshold are tunable but the fusion structure is theoretically motivated. The failure mode unique to this fusion is signal correlation: position-level rejection variance and aggregate acceptance rate are not independent, so treating them as such in a naive Bayesian update inflates confidence in changepoint detection; a cleaner implementation orthogonalizes them by regressing out the acceptance rate trend from the position variance series before fusing, analogous to factor model residualization. For sudden swaps specifically, there's an additional practical lever: if the serving infrastructure knows a target model swap occurred (it usually does, since it controls deployment), that event should be injected as a hard prior reset rather than inferred from signals, reducing detection latency from hundreds of tokens to zero and making the statistical machinery relevant only for the gradual drift case where no such oracle exists.

The theoretically sound fallback during the warm-up gap is to treat speculation as a biased proposal mechanism rather than an exact acceleration scheme — specifically, revert to a very short window (γ=1 or 2) with a modified acceptance criterion that applies a temperature correction to the draft logits, effectively widening the acceptance region to tolerate higher draft-target KL at the cost of slight output distribution distortion that vanishes as the draft adapts. This is theoretically grounded in the token-level rejection sampling view of speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023): the standard acceptance criterion preserves the target distribution exactly, but a relaxed criterion that accepts with probability min(1, (1+ε)·p_target/p_draft) introduces bounded bias proportional to ε while maintaining higher acceptance rates during mismatch — you're trading distribution fidelity for throughput continuity, and ε can be annealed to zero as warm-up data accumulates. The warm-up gap length itself is estimable: empirically, Online Speculative Decoding finds that ~500-1000 accepted tokens of fine-tuning signal suffice for LoRA-based draft adaptation to stabilize, suggesting the fallback regime needs to cover roughly that many verification steps before the neural draft is trustworthy again — at 4-8 tokens per speculative step, that's 60-250 requests at typical prompt lengths. The system-level architecture that makes this clean is a draft ensemble that maintains both the stale neural draft and the retrieval fallback simultaneously, routing to whichever produces higher estimated acceptance probability on a per-request basis using the cheap proxy signal of draft-target logit agreement on the first token — this avoids hard switching logic and naturally transitions back to the neural draft as it warms up without a discrete handoff.

The core filtering mechanism should be a confidence gate on datastore writes: only commit a (context, continuation) pair to the retrieval store if the target model's own log-probability of the continuation exceeds a threshold, since low-quality or transitional outputs will tend to have diffuse target distributions (high entropy) that the target itself assigns low likelihood — this is self-supervised and requires no external quality signal. For capability updates, the poisoning risk is primarily capability regression artifacts: the new target may produce outputs that are stylistically or factually different from the old target in ways that are correct for the new regime but would confuse the retrieval draft if mixed with old-regime entries, so the right policy is a hard datastore flush at swap time followed by gated writes, accepting that the store starts empty and builds cleanly rather than inheriting contaminated history. Safety patches create a qualitatively different problem: the transitional outputs that are most dangerous to store are precisely the ones the patch was designed to eliminate — refusal bypasses, harmful completions, format violations — and these may have high target log-probability under the pre-patch model that briefly persists in serving before the swap fully propagates, meaning the confidence gate fails because the old model confidently endorses what the new model would reject. The solution for safety patches specifically is to augment the confidence gate with a consistency check against the new target's safety classifier or a lightweight reward model: only write entries where both the token-level confidence gate passes and the completion scores above a safety threshold, effectively requiring dual approval — this mirrors how Constitutional AI filtering works at training time but applied here at inference-time datastore curation. Operationally, this distinction means the serving infrastructure needs to know why a swap occurred, not just that it occurred — a metadata flag (capability vs. safety) should propagate to the datastore manager to switch between flush-and-rebuild (capability) versus flush-plus-dual-gate (safety) policies, and the warm-up period for safety patches should be treated as strictly longer because a poisoned safety-relevant entry that slips through can cause the retrieval draft to propose harmful tokens that the target then rejects, leaking latency and potentially surfacing the rejected content to downstream logging systems.

For low-frequency distributions where the retrieval datastore stays permanently sparse, the right architecture is a tiered draft system that falls back through a hierarchy: retrieval draft first (when store density exceeds a per-query threshold, e.g., fewer than k=5 near-neighbors within a cosine distance cutoff), then a domain-specialized small neural draft, then a universal draft with shortened γ — with the tier selection made per-request at negligible cost by checking store density before committing to a speculative path. The domain-specialized small neural draft tier is more tractable than it sounds for rare languages and specialized domains because of the asymmetry between draft and target size: a 1-3B parameter draft fine-tuned on, say, medical Swahili or legal Cantonese requires far less data to achieve useful acceptance rates than fine-tuning the 70B+ target, and distillation from the target's logits on a small synthetic corpus (500-2000 examples, generated by the target itself) can produce a viable draft even for distributions the target sees rarely. This synthetic corpus approach is what LLMWare and several medical deployment systems use implicitly when they distill domain drafts, though they rarely publish acceptance rate numbers — the key insight is that you don't need the draft to match the target globally, only on the specific conditional distributions that arise from the rare domain's prompt patterns, which are far more constrained than the full distribution. The failure mode unique to permanently sparse stores is retrieval hallucination: when k-NN search returns neighbors that are superficially similar (same script, same domain keywords) but semantically distant, the retrieval draft proposes tokens from an unrelated context that happen to share surface features — this is worse than a neural draft's failures because it's confidently wrong in structured ways that cascade through the speculative window. The theoretically cleanest solution for permanently low-frequency distributions is to abandon retrieval entirely for those query types and instead use prompt-conditioned draft modulation: steer the universal draft at inference time using a lightweight adapter (a few hundred parameters) conditioned on a domain embedding of the current prompt, so the draft shifts toward the target's domain-specific distribution without requiring a separate fine-tuned model per domain — this is architecturally similar to what mixture-of-experts routing does at training time, applied here to draft proposal at serving time.
